rows.description: A child whose parents respond only to marks feels loved for performance and hides mistakes; the harm is less the standard than the sense that love depends on meeting it.
A teenager studies late, procrastinates from dread of not doing it well enough and feels empty after a good result. Standards move higher each time, and joy disappears from effort.
A child whose parents respond only to marks feels loved for performance and hides mistakes; the harm is less the standard than the sense that love depends on meeting it.
A teacher notes a student who never turns in drafts and cries over a small mark. Praising the effort, letting the student see teachers' own mistakes and allowing messy first tries reduce the fear.
A child who fears being wrong will only do puzzles they already know how to solve; avoiding failure feels safe but also blocks learning.
I refuse to try things I might fail at. Wise: fear of failure limits me more than failure does; start with low-stakes attempts.
A child says a project will be quick and starts the night before. He imagines the ideal path and forgets past delays.

rows.subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
rows.description: A parent watches a teenager cram a project the night before and recognises the pattern of underestimating. Rather than rescuing every time, a wise parent lets small consequences teach while helping build a starting routine.
A child who spelled one word wrong on a test declares the whole test a disaster and says they are stupid; anything short of perfect is filed as total failure.
A young adult starts an ambitious fitness or study routine with great energy and quits after the first missed day. All-or-nothing thinking turns one lapse into a reason to abandon everything.
A child says a project will be quick and starts the night before. He imagines the ideal path and forgets past delays.

rows.subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
rows.description: A student who has run late on every previous assignment still expects this one to be different. Knowing about the fallacy does not remove it; the optimistic picture feels like a special case each time.
